claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among single-phase FCC equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets originate from composition-dependent local lattice distortions and solute clustering.
Local lattice distortions and solute clustering modify dislocation mobility.
Changes in dislocation mobility govern differences in yield strength and work-hardening behavior.
Identical thermomechanical processing can isolate composition effects when comparing the quinary alloy with its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The proposed comparison is restricted to single-phase FCC alloys in a temperature range where dislocation glide dominates and no phase transformation occurs.
Atomic size and electronic differences among constituent elements induce lattice distortions.
These lattice distortions increase resistance to dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
Reducing the number of components may change the magnitude and spatial pervasiveness of lattice distortion.
Reducing chemical complexity may change the degree of local solute clustering.
Local solute clustering can modulate mechanical response.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, the quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit reduced yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit distinct work-hardening rates.
Reduced yield strength and altered work hardening will correlate with reduced lattice-distortion intensity and altered solute clustering.
X-ray diffraction line broadening can be used to quantify lattice distortion in these alloys.
Atom probe tomography or an equivalent technique can assess solute clustering in these alloys.
A lack of systematic correlation between mechanical-property differences and lattice distortion or solute clustering would falsify the hypothesis.
